The Amitābha Sutra is the essential teaching that the World-Honored One proclaimed without being asked, the profound sutra praised by the Buddhas of the ten directions, the wondrous Dharma of ultimate expedience, the consummate goal of perfect and sudden instruction. It is the most important scripture of the Pure Land school, called the First Sutra of the Pure Land, for in it Śākyamuni Buddha praises the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss and reveals
the certain rebirth
in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss through
the path of liberation in this very life

. This path is praised with one voice by the Buddhas of the ten directions (including, of course, Amitābha Buddha of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss). Those who deeply give rise to faith and understanding will surely be received and protected by the Buddhas of the ten directions (including, of course, Amitābha Buddha of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss); those who practice as instructed will surely be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. The sutra says:
(The Buddhas of the ten directions)
each manifest the broad and long tongue, spreading it over the three-thousand great-thousand world, and, circling it all around, speak words of truth: ‘You sentient beings,
should all faithfully accept
this teaching of ‘praise of the merits of the inconceivable Buddha-land, the Dharma-gate received by all Buddhas,’
The Dharma-gate

“If a good man or good woman, whether already having heard, or about to hear, or now hearing, has heard this sutra and deeply gives rise to faith and understanding.
Having given rise to faith and understanding,
they will surely be
received by such Tathagatas dwelling in the ten directions, [in number like] the sands of ten Ganges

received and protected

will surely

in the pure Buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitayus.”

[The path of liberation in this very life] is the path by which, in this very life, one ends birth-and-death and escapes the three realms. Through the ordinary paths of practice, to end birth-and-death and escape the three realms one must completely eradicate afflictions; this is extremely difficult and all but impossible to reach within this very life. And if in this life one cannot end birth-and-death and escape the three realms, then, because of the delusion of passing from one birth to the next, no one knows in which life and in which kalpa one will again set foot upon the bodhi path. Yet the Buddha-recitation path that the World-Honored One reveals here needs only a mind held fast without confusion; at the moment of death one is certainly reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, thereby ending birth-and-death and escaping the three realms. This is something anyone can attain within this very life, so long as the method is correct and one strives with sincere and unremitting effort. Hence it is called the path of liberation in this very life, praised with one voice by the Buddhas of the ten directions. Those who deeply give rise to faith and understanding are surely received and protected by the Buddhas of the ten directions; those who practice as taught are surely reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. [The delusion of passing from one birth to the next] means forgetting everything at rebirth.

The Amitābha Sutra exists in two translations. One is the Sutra of the Buddha Speaks of Amitābha, translated by the great master Kumarajiva during the Yao Qin period, commonly called the Qin translation; the other is the Sutra of Praise for the Pure Land Buddha’s Reception of Beings, translated by the great master Xuanzang in the Tang dynasty, commonly called the Tang translation.

Responding to the Chinese people’s preference for concision, Master Kumarajiva translated chiefly by meaning: the text is brief yet rich in import, subtle and fluent. Master Xuanzang, in order to preserve the original appearance, translated word for word: accurate and complete, the original expressions retained, the wording clear and detailed, free of the faults of misunderstanding and invention, which is of vital importance for study and practice. When one studies the meaning of the sutra closely and sets the two translations side by side, one can reach a deeper and more accurate understanding.
For example, in the Sutra of the Buddha Speaks of Amitābha:

“Sariputra, if a good man or good woman hears this Amitābha Buddha and holds fast to his name, for one day, or two days, or three, or four, or five, or six, or seven days, with a single mind without confusion, then at the end of life that person, with Amitābha Buddha and the holy assembly now appearing before him, will have a mind not inverted; at death he will be reborn in the supremely blissful land of Amitābha Buddha.”
In this passage there are two questions of deep concern to students of the Pure Land:
First, what is “a single mind without confusion”? For a long time there have been many conflicting views and endless debate.

Second, regarding the phrase “at the end of life, with a mind not inverted,” people often ask: in order to be reborn freely, must one, besides reaching a single mind without confusion, also avoid an inverted mind at the moment the four great elements dissolve at death?
The Sutra of Praise for the Pure Land Buddha’s Reception of Beings translates it thus:

“Sariputra, the pure-hearted good man or good woman who hears the name of Amitayus, the Tathagata, with its immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable merits, and the adorned merits of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, and, having heard, reflects upon them; for one day or night, or two or three, or four or five, or six or seven, holds the mind without confusion. When that good man or good woman comes to the end of life, Amitayus Buddha, together with his countless sravaka disciples and the bodhisattvas, gathers before him, surrounding him front and back, and with compassionate protection causes his mind to be undisturbed. Having already abandoned life, he follows the Buddha’s assembly and is born in the pure Buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitayus.”
Setting the two side by side, it becomes clear:
First, “a single mind without confusion” is “held a mind without confusion.”

Second, “at the end of life, with a mind not inverted” is joined to the preceding phrase “Amitābha Buddha and the holy assembly now appearing before him,” meaning: Amitābha Buddha and the holy assembly appear before him and, with compassionate protection, cause his mind not to be inverted. That is to say, so long as one induces Amitābha Buddha to appear and receive one, even when the four great elements dissolve and the suffering presses in and maras appear, because of Amitābha Buddha’s compassionate protection, one’s mind will not be inverted.

A special word should be said: the Heart Sutra translated by Master Xuanzang is universally loved and known in every household, reaching everywhere without limit. The Sutra of Praise for the Pure Land Buddha’s Reception of Beings that he translated is also rendered with consummate skill—not only accurate and complete, its meaning detailed and its reasoning lucid, its literary polish brilliant, but it reads smoothly and trippingly on the tongue, attaining the highest realm of the translator’s art—faithfulness, fluency, and elegance—and possessing an extraordinarily powerful power to draw and hold the reader.

[Faithfulness, fluency, and elegance] For a translated work, to be wholly faithful to the original, accurate and complete, is called “faithfulness”; to be fluent in wording, “fluency”; to be brilliant in literary polish, “elegance.”
[The Sutra of Praise for the Pure Land Buddha’s Reception of Beings]

the title, ‘Praise of the Pure Land Buddha’s Reception of Beings,’ means that this sutra praises the merits of the inconceivable Buddha-land of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, and is the Dharma-gate received and protected by the Buddhas of the ten directions. In the sutra the Buddha says:

“Sariputra, for what reason is this sutra named ‘praise of the merits of the inconceivable Buddha-land, the Dharma-gate received by all Buddhas’? Sariputra, because in this sutra the merits of the inconceivable Buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitayus, and the Buddhas and World-Honored Ones of the ten directions, desiring by expeditious means to benefit and bring peace and joy to all sentient beings, each, abiding in his own land, display great miraculous transformations and speak words of truth, urging all sentient beings to faithfully accept this teaching. Therefore this sutra is named
‘praise of the merits of the inconceivable Buddha-land, the Dharma-gate received by all Buddhas.’”

In this sutra, Śākyamuni Buddha praises the merits of the inconceivable Buddha-land of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss: the adornment of its environment, the adornment of its inhabitants; the absence of all suffering and the enjoyment of every happiness; immeasurable lifespan; meeting with hosts of all the highest good; and, never regressing, going on to Buddhahood. He likewise teaches the practice-path received by all Buddhas: holding the mind without confusion, and so being reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss and passing beyond birth-and-death horizontally. In the sutra the Buddha says:

“The pure-hearted good man or good woman who hears the name of Amitayus, the Tathagata, with its immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable merits, and the adorned merits of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, and, having heard, reflects upon them; for one day or night, or two or three, or four or five, or six or seven, holds the mind without confusion. When that good man or good woman comes to the end of life, Amitayus Buddha, together with his countless sravaka disciples and the bodhisattvas, gathers before him, surrounding him front and back, and with compassionate protection causes his mind to be undisturbed. Having already abandoned life, he follows the Buddha’s assembly and is born in the pure Buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitayus.”
The essential teaching of this sutra:
with faith and acceptance, make vows, practice as instructed, hold the mind without confusion, and be born in that Buddha-land.
In the sutra the World-Honored One says:

“The pure-hearted good man or good woman who hears the name of Amitayus, the Tathagata, with its immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable merits, and the adorned merits of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, and, having heard, reflects upon them; for one day or night, or two or three, or four or five, or six or seven,

Having already abandoned life, he follows the Buddha’s assembly and is born in the pure Buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitayus.”

the Dharma-gate received by all Buddhas, and the World-Honored One in this sutra concretely and clearly teaches how to cultivate this Dharma-gate.

, and be born in that Buddha-land

Here the Buddha sets out faith, vows, and practice with complete clarity: faith is “faithfully accepting” the World-Honored One’s teaching above; the vow is making the vow “to practice as instructed and be born in that Buddha-land”; practice is practicing as instructed, holding the mind without confusion.

While faith and vows remain only in the head, they are merely a notion. Faith and vows must be practiced and carried out; only then are they genuine faith and sincere vows. Therefore genuine faith and sincere vows necessarily lead to vigorous practice. Without truly diligent cultivation, how can one verify what one believes? How can one fulfill what one has vowed? Faith and vows without practice are nothing but empty faith and idle vows.
In this sutra, the World-Honored One, over and over, time and again, stresses the need to “
practice as instructed

,” and clearly teaches: so long as one practices as instructed, one is received by the Buddhas of the ten directions, is surely reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, never regresses, and quickly attains the Buddha-fruit. His concern overflows in his words; the World-Honored One teaches:

“The pure-hearted good man or good woman who hears the name of Amitayus, the Tathagata, with its inconceivable merits, and the pure Buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, should all with faith and acceptance make the vow,
practice as instructed

“In this defiled, enduring world of the five turbid and evil times, the pure-hearted good man or good woman who hears this teaching so hard to believe in all the world, and can give rise to faith and understanding, accept, uphold, proclaim, and

, should be known as one most rare, who in immeasurable Buddha-fields has planted good roots. When such a person ends life, he is surely reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, where he enjoys the various Mahayana joys of the adorned, pure Buddha-land.”
Therefore the student must deeply believe and grasp the meaning of “
practice as instructed
” and put it into action, zealous day after day, pressing forward without pause.
[Zealous] Diligent and untiring.

The most striking feature of this sutra is: praised by the Buddhas of the ten directions, received by all Buddhas, passing beyond birth-and-death horizontally, never regressing, and attaining Buddhahood in a single lifetime.
[Praised by the Buddhas of the ten directions]:
The sutra says:
(The Buddhas of the ten directions)

each manifest the broad and long tongue, spreading it over the three-thousand great-thousand world, and, circling it all around, speak words of truth: ‘You sentient beings, you should all faithfully accept this teaching of ‘praise of the merits of the inconceivable Buddha-land, the Dharma-gate received by all Buddhas.’”
[Received by all Buddhas]:
The sutra says:

“If a good man or good woman, whether already having heard, or about to hear, or now hearing, has heard this sutra and deeply gives rise to faith and understanding. Having given rise to faith and understanding, he will surely be received by such Tathagatas dwelling in the ten directions, [in number like] the sands of ten Ganges
(Ganges)
-rivers of Buddhas and World-Honored Ones.”
[Passing beyond birth-and-death horizontally]
Master Yinguang says:

“Why is Buddha-recitation, seeking rebirth in the West, called the horizontally-transcending path? The ancients had a simile to explain it: they liken an ordinary being replete with delusion and karma to a worm born in the lowest joint of a bamboo, and this bamboo to the three realms. The worm wants to get out by only two means: one is to bore straight up, the other to bore straight across. To bore straight up means, from the lowest stage, to gnaw through joint after joint, and only when the topmost joint is pierced can it come out. This likens
(the simile)
cultivating other paths, which require eradicating all the views and thought afflictions before one can emerge from the three realms
(only then can one escape the three realms and end birth-and-death)

. The view delusions number eighty-eight, the thought delusions eighty-one grades; these many grades are likened to the joints of a bamboo. The worm boring straight up is called the vertical emergence. For example, a sage of the first fruit who has cut off the view delusions must pass through seven births in heaven and seven births among humans, through long kalpas of cultivation, before he can realize arhatship and end birth-and-death. One of the second fruit must likewise pass once through heaven and once among humans before realizing the fourth fruit. One of the third fruit, having already exhausted the thought delusions of the desire realm, must still, in the five no-return heavens, gradually cultivate before he can exhaust the thought delusions and realize the fourth fruit. Only then is he a non-learner sage who has left the three realms. If one of the third fruit is of dull faculties, he must further be born in the four formless heavens, from the heaven of the sphere of infinite space up to the heaven of neither perception nor non-perception, before he can realize the fourth fruit. This vertical path is thus arduous and long-drawn-out. To bore straight across is for this worm, instead of boring through joint by joint, simply to gnaw a hole straight sideways and so come out. Such a method is far easier than the vertical one. Those who recite the Buddha’s name are likewise. Though they have not eradicated the views and thought afflictions
(the views and thought delusions)

, yet if they can be complete in the three provisions of the Pure Land—faith, vows, and practice—then at death they can influence Amitābha Buddha to come and receive them, to be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Once in that pure land, the views and thought afflictions are cut off of themselves. Why? Because the land’s environment is supreme and its conditions are strong, so there are no conditions that stir up afflictions in people. Thus one attains the three non-regressions, until he has broken through the dust-mote-like
(dust-mote delusions)
ignorance
(ignorance delusions)
, and realizes supreme bodhi
(Buddhahood)

—how direct and easy a matter! Hence the ancients say, studying the Way through other paths is like an ant climbing a high mountain; Buddha-recitation and rebirth in the West is like a sailboat riding the current.”
(From Talks on Returning to Lingyan from Shanghai)

[The three realms] The desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm. The desire realm is the world where beings possessed of the two desires of sex and food dwell, including above the six heavens of desire, in the middle humans and animals, and below the hungry ghosts and hells. The form realm is the world of beings who, without the two desires of sex and food, still have a body of form, including the eighteen heavens of the four meditations. The formless realm is the world of beings who have no body of form but abide in mind-consciousness in deep meditative concentration, including the four heavens of formlessness (the heaven of infinite space, the heaven of infinite consciousness, the heaven of nothingness, and the heaven of neither perception nor non-perception). These three realms are all the round of birth-and-death for ordinary beings, so the first aim of the Buddhist practitioner is to escape the three realms.
[The three non-regressions]

First, non-regression of stage, the stage one has attained is not lost; second, non-regression of practice, one does not fall away from the practice one has undertaken; third, non-regression of mindfulness, one does not turn back from right mindfulness. [The views and thought delusions] The view delusions and the thought delusions. The view delusions are the deluded errors of ordinary beings in their views, such as the view of self, the view of extremes, the perverse view, the view of attachments, and the view of moral prohibitions and precepts, the five wrong views. The thought delusions are the deluded errors of ordinary beings in their thoughts, such as greed, anger, delusion, pride, and doubt. These two delusions are the root cause of sentient beings wandering in the three realms to undergo birth-and-death fruitlessly; cutting them off enables one to end birth-and-death and escape the three realms. [The dust-mote delusions] The dust-mote delusions are the delusions of bodhisattvas. If a bodhisattva, in saving sentient beings, has not mastered the countless Dharma-gates like dust and sand, he cannot complete the work of teaching sentient beings; hence they are called the dust-mote delusions. [The ignorance delusions] The ignorance delusion is the fundamental ignorance that can obscure the principle of the ultimate reality of the Middle Way; cut it off completely and one becomes a Buddha.
[Never regressing]
The sutra says:
“All beings born in that land never regress.”
[Attaining Buddhahood in a single lifetime]
The sutra says:
“All beings born in that land never regress, and will never fall again into the evil destinies, border regions, lowly outcast
(lowly castes)
among them; they constantly roam the pure Buddha-lands of all Buddhas, and their supreme practices and vows advance with every thought, and they are certain to realize anuttara-samyak-sambodhi
(Buddhahood)
[Translated by imperial command by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang]

[Tripitaka Master] “Tripitaka” means the sutra-pitaka, the vinaya-pitaka, and the abhidharma-pitaka. The sutra-pitaka consists of the scriptures spoken by the Buddha; the vinaya-pitaka, of the precepts laid down by the Buddha; the abhidharma-pitaka, of the treatises composed by the Buddha’s disciples. A “Tripitaka Master” is a monk who is thoroughly versed in all three pitakas. [Xuanzang] Master Xuanzang (

), a celebrated Tripitaka Master of the Tang dynasty, is ranked with Kumarajiva and Paramartha as one of the three great translators of Chinese Buddhism, and was one of the founders of the Consciousness-only school. [Translated by imperial command] Master Xuanzang translated this sutra by order of Emperor Taizong of the Tang.

Master Xuanzang was born in the second year of the Renshou era of the Sui dynasty. As a child he followed his elder brother, the Dharma Master Changjie, to live at Jidu Monastery [sic] in Luoyang, where he studied Buddhism. At eleven (
) he already read fluently the Lotus Sutra and the Vimalakirti Sutra. At thirteen (

), when Luoyang held the examination for ordaining monks, though still young, he was chosen out of the ordinary because of his outstanding examination results. Afterwards he heard the Dharma Master Jing lecture on the Nirvāṇa Sutra, learned the Compendium from the Dharma Master Yan, and, ascending the seat to repeat the teaching, analyzed it in detail, winning the admiration of the assembly.

[The examination for ordaining monks] In ancient times, the court established a system of ordaining monks to control the number of monks and nuns, to ensure their quality, and to forbid private ordination. It was stipulated that anyone seeking to leave home must pass an examination on the Buddhist scriptures before being permitted to shave and be ordained.

Later, Master Xuanzang traveled to various places to study, and soon exhausted the doctrines of every school; his ability was highly praised and his fame filled the capital. The President of the Department of State Affairs, Xiao Yu, memorialized the throne asking that he be settled at Zhuangyan Monastery. Because he felt deeply that the various teachings he had heard over many years in different places were inconsistent, and especially that the two schools current at the time, the She-lun school (later absorbed into the Dharma-character school) and the Di-lun school, disagreed greatly on the characteristics of phenomena, he longed for the Yogacarabhumi Sastra, which gathers together the teachings of the three vehicles, in order to fuse and unify all of it, and so resolved to go to India to seek the Dharma.
Because he could not obtain the travel permit (passport) issued by the Tang court, he never fulfilled his wish. In

years old), Master Xuanzang determinedly set out on his own from Chang’an, risking the journey to Tianzhu (present-day India). Under extraordinarily dangerous and arduous conditions, with an unyielding heroic spirit, he overcame countless difficulties and perils and finally reached Tianzhu.

During his more than ten years in Tianzhu, Master Xuanzang attended and consulted many famous eminent monks. Among the monasteries where he stayed was the great center of Buddhist learning of that era, Nalanda Monastery. He studied the Yogacarabhumi Sastra and the other sutras and treatises under that monastery’s abbot, the great Indian Buddhist authority, the Dharma Master Silabhadra. Silabhadra was a disciple of Dharmapala and a grand-disciple of Vasubandhu. In the thirteenth year of the Zhenguan era, Master Xuanzang lectured on the Mahayanasamgraha and the Vijnaptimatrata-siddhi on behalf of the Dharma Master Silabhadra at Nalanda. Afterward, he also traveled on foot throughout the whole of the South Asian subcontinent.

Master Xuanzang was not only profoundly versed in the Buddha-Dharma but also skilled in Sanskrit, so he took part repeatedly in religious debate assemblies and won them all, his reputation rising daily. At the invitation of the King of Magadha, Harsha, he presided over the great open debate assembly at Kanyakubja, extolling the Mahayana teaching. Present were the kings of eighteen countries, more than three thousand monks of both the Greater and Lesser Vehicles, more than two thousand Brahmins and heterodox disputants, and over a thousand monks of Nalanda. The Master took the seat of the main disputant and addressed the assembly, declaring: “If there is in my words a single phrase without reason, and anyone can refute it, I beg that my head be cut off [in atonement].” He waited eighteen days, and in the end no one dared come forward to dispute, so he won without a battle. When the assembly dispersed, all were greatly delighted, exclaiming that such a thing had never been seen. Thus his fame rose like a thunderclap and shook all of Tianzhu. The Mahayanists called him Mahayana Deva (Deva of the Great Vehicle), the Hinayanists called him Moksa Deva (Deva of Liberation), and King Harsha bowed to him as his teacher.
, Master Xuanzang set out homeward laden with honors, and brought
works of Buddhist scripture back to China. In
, he returned to Chang’an, where he was warmly received and comforted by Emperor Taizong. In

, in the western courtyard of the Ci’en Monastery within Chang’an, Master Xuanzang built a five-story pagoda (the present-day Giant Wild Goose Pagoda), to store the scriptures and images he had brought back from Tianzhu. In

, a memorial hall to Master Xuanzang was established in the monastery. The Giant Wild Goose Pagoda became an architectural memorial to Master Xuanzang’s westward journey in search of the Dharma and his translation of the scriptures upon his return.

With the vigorous support of Emperor Taizong, Master Xuanzang established a scripture-translation institute (a state translation bureau) in Chang’an, where outstanding scholars from all over the country and from East Asian lands took part in translation. He spent more than ten years, within the Yuhua Palace, rendering a great many scriptures into Chinese. These Buddhist scriptures were later transmitted from China to the Korean peninsula, Vietnam, and Japan.

Master Xuanzang, through his translation of the Buddhist scriptures and his exegesis of their texts, founded the Chinese Faxiang (Consciousness-Only) school; yet his teachings deeply influenced many other schools.

Over his lifetime the Master translated seventy-four works in all, one thousand three hundred and thirty-eight fascicles, including the six hundred fascicles of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sutra — more than any other translator of the Middle Kingdom. Through Master Xuanzang's westward quest for the Dharma, tracing it to its very source, Chinese Buddhism obtained the complete essential meaning of the Buddha's teaching, and from then on it flourished in China.
The Master passed away in the first year of the Linde era, on the fifth day of the second month (
), and was buried on the White Deer Plain. Tens of thousands attended the funeral; the emperor (Gaozong of Tang), overcome with grief, wept aloud and held no court for three days.
Note: the headings of the following sections are the analytical divisions of the text and do not belong to the sutra itself.

blocks.text: 1. The Sacred Assembly at the Dharma-gathering

inline.s: “Thus have I heard: at one time the Bhagavat dwelt at Shravasti, in the Jetavana Grove, the garden of the Benign and Giver of Alms.”
This is what I (Ānanda) heard with my own ears
: at that time the Buddha was in the country of Shravasti (
the Kingdom of Kosala
), dwelling in the Jetavana Grove, the garden of the Benign and Giver of Alms (
the Jetavana, the Grove of the Giver of Alms, temple-garden of Anathapindada
“Thus have I heard” — this is what I (Ānanda) heard personally. This sutra was recounted by Ānanda, the disciple of Śākyamuni Buddha, at the time the scriptures were compiled in council.

“Ānanda” — his full name is Anandatta; he is one of the Buddha's ten great disciples. He was the Buddha's cousin, born on the very night the Buddha attained enlightenment, and afterwards left home under the Buddha and served him for twenty-five years as his personal attendant. He was renowned as foremost in learning, and many scriptures were recited by him at the council. “The ten great disciples” — the Buddha's ten great disciples are: Shariputra, foremost in wisdom; Maudgalyayana, foremost in psychic powers; Subhuti, foremost in understanding emptiness; Ānanda, foremost in learning; Upali, foremost in observing the precepts; Aniruddha, foremost in the divine eye; Mahakasyapa, foremost in ascetic practice; Purna, foremost in preaching; Katyayana, foremost in discussion; and Rahula, foremost in secret conduct. “Ascetic practice” — the method of casting aside the three attachments to clothing, food, and lodging. He who practices the ascetic ways must observe twelve rules, called the “twelve dhutas.” “At one time” — at that time.

“Bhagavat” — an honorific title of the Buddha. “Shravasti” — that is, the Kingdom of Kosala. “The Jetavana Grove, the garden of the Benign and Giver of Alms” — this is the “Jetavana Grove, the garden of the Giver of Alms” in the Sutra on the Buddha Amitābha; it was a park in the capital city of the Kingdom of Kosala (Shravasti), and there Śākyamuni Buddha spoke this sutra.

“Together with the great assembly of bhikshus, twelve hundred and fifty in all. These were all venerable hearer-disciples, well known to the assembly, great arhats. Their names are: the venerable Shariputra, Mahamaudgalyayana, Mahakasyapa, and Aniruddha. Great hearers such as these were at the head.”

“They were together with twelve hundred and fifty great bhikshus. All were hearer-disciples of venerable age and virtue, great arhats well known to everyone. Among them the venerables Shariputra, Mahamaudgalyayana, Mahakasyapa and Aniruddha, and other such great hearer-disciples, held the highest position.”
“Bhikshu (bì chú)”

— that is, a bhikshu: a renunciate who has received the full precepts. Among such, a man is called a bhikshu and a woman a bhikshuni. The term “great bhikshu” describes that these monks were all of very high attainment. “Together” — in one place. “Hearer” — one who hears the sound of the Buddha's teaching of the Four Noble Truths and awakens to the Way. “Truth” — a principle that is true and free from error. “The Four Noble Truths” — the truth of suffering, the truth of its arising, the truth of its cessation, and the truth of the path. First, “the truth of suffering” is the truth that life is beset with much suffering. Second, “the truth of its arising” is the truth of whence the suffering of life comes; the “arising” in “truth of arising” means to draw together and to occasion. Third, “the truth of cessation” is the truth of the extinction of all suffering. Fourth, “the truth of the path” is the truth of how one may forever put an end to the arising of suffering, that is, the way of ceasing suffering. Among the Four Noble Truths, arising is the cause and suffering its effect; the path is the cause and cessation its effect. “Venerable” — an honorific for an arhat. “At the head” — the position of highest rank within the assembly.

“He was likewise together with immeasurable bodhisattva-mahasattvas, all abiding in the stage of non-retrogression, adorned with countless merits. Their names are: the bodhisattva Manjushri, the bodhisattva Ajita, the bodhisattva Constant Effort, the bodhisattva Never Resting. Great bodhisattvas such as these were at the head.”
“He was also together with immeasurable great bodhisattvas, all abiding in the stage of non-retrogression, endowed with countless merits and all manner of adornments. Among them
the bodhisattva Manjushri
the bodhisattva Maitreya
, the bodhisattva Constant Effort, the bodhisattva Never Resting, and other such great bodhisattvas, held the highest position.”

“Bodhisattva-mahasattva” — bodhisattvas have various grades, high, middle and low; to indicate the bodhisattvas who dwell on the stages, one adds the word “mahasattva.” The Discourse on Buddhahood says: “We take here the great bodhisattvas who dwell on the stages; therefore the word ‘mahasattva’ is added.” So “bodhisattva-mahasattva” denotes a bodhisattva of the stages. “Bodhisattva of the stages” — in passing from ordinary person to Buddhahood, a bodhisattva goes through fifty-two stages: the ten faiths, the ten abidings, the ten practices, the ten dedications, the ten stages, the stage of equal enlightenment, and the stage of wondrous enlightenment. The bodhisattvas dwelling on the ten stages are called bodhisattvas of the stages. “State of non-retrogression” — the merit and good roots that are cultivated only increase and advance and never again regress; this is the Sanskrit avivartika. “The bodhisattva Manjushri” — that is, the bodhisattva Manjushri. “The bodhisattva Ajita” — that is, the Ajita bodhisattva (Maitreya) in the Sutra on the Buddha Amitābha.

“There were also Shakra, and the Great Brahma king, lord of the world of endurance, and the four kings who guard the world — such as these were at the head. Hundreds of thousands of crores of nayutas of hosts of sons of the gods, and likewise countless gods and humans and asuras of the world, all came and sat in the assembly for the sake of hearing the Dharma.”

“There were also hundreds of thousands of millions of the gods of the heavens, and countless gods and humans and asuras of the world, who all came to the Dharma-gathering for the sake of hearing the Dharma. Among them
Shakra, king of the Trayastrimsa heaven
, the Great Brahma king, lord of the saha world, and the four great kings — such as these held the highest position.”

“Shakra” — that is, Shakra Devanam Indra, the king of the Trayastrimsa heaven, the second of the heavens. “The Great Brahma king” — the king of the Brahma heavens, lord of the saha world. The Sutra on Dependent Arising Spoken by the Buddha says: “At that time the Great Brahma king, lord of the saha world, by the Buddha's power, knew what the Buddha was contemplating. Just as a mighty man bends and extends his arm, he left the Brahma world and came to where the Buddha was. Having made his reverent salutations, he stood before the Buddha and said: ‘World-Honored One! What the Buddha is contemplating is just so: the suffering and joy of the world, from which none can escape — this is a great benefit and meaning, and so also in past and future. In the realms of gods, humans, demons, and Brahma, the World-Honored One alone knows each and every thing, whether increasing or decreasing, whether good or evil, and can distinguish them all; and the Dharma of dependent arising he knows as it truly is, through the power of Buddha-wisdom.’” “The world of endurance” — that is, the world of endurance, also named the saha world (“saha” is rendered in Chinese as “enduring”). Because the beings of this world can bear to endure the ten evil acts, the three poisons and all the afflictions without being willing to leave, it is called the “world of endurance,” or for short the “realm of forbearance.” “Lord of the world of endurance” — the lord of the saha world, that is, the Great Brahma king. “The four kings who guard the world” — that is, the four great kings: the eastern king who sustains the realm, the southern king who increases growth, the western king who gazes far, and the northern king who hears much; these are the benevolent gods who protect the saha world. “Koti (
zhī

) and nayuta” — a hundred million times a hundred million. “Koti,” also written kotih, is rendered “a crore” (ten million); “nayuta,” also written nayutas, corresponds to a hundred million in this land. “Sons of the gods” — the gods of heaven. “Asuras” — that is, asuras. “And likewise the countless gods, humans and asuras of the world” — moreover there are the immeasurable gods of the world (referring to the various world-gods), asuras, and so on.
“Then the World-Honored One said to Shariputra: Do you now know
(to be read ‘no’?)

? To the west of here, passing beyond hundreds of thousands of crores of nayutas of Buddha-lands, there is a Buddha-world called Ultimate Bliss. Its World-Honored One is named Measureless Life and Measureless Light, Tathagata, Worthy of Offerings, Fully and Rightly Enlightened, with the ten titles complete. He is now there, dwelling securely, and speaks for living beings the profound, subtle and wonderful Dharma, causing them to attain supreme benefit and bliss.”

“At this the Buddha told Shariputra: Do you know? Going west from this world, passing beyond hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddha-lands, there is a Buddha-world called Ultimate Bliss. Its Buddha is named Measureless Life, and Measureless Light; he is fully complete with the ten titles, Tathagata, Worthy of Offerings, Fully and Rightly Enlightened, and so on. He is now there, dwelling securely, and speaks for the many beings the profound, subtle and wonderful Dharma, causing them to attain supreme benefit and bliss.”

“World-Honored One” — an honorific of the Buddha, because the Buddha is the one revered by all the world. “Shariputra” — that is, Shariputra. “Tathagata, Worthy of Offerings, Fully and Rightly Enlightened” — Tathagata, Worthy of Offerings, Fully and Rightly Enlightened. “Fully and Rightly Enlightened” — true, universal and equal enlightenment, that is, the enlightenment of the Buddha. “The ten titles” — the Buddha has ten honorific titles: first, Tathagata, who comes by the way of reality to perfect enlightenment; second, Worthy of Offerings, worthy of the offerings of gods and humans; third, Universally and Rightly Knowing, truly knowing all things; fourth, Endowed with Clear Knowledge and Conduct, complete with the three clear knowledges (knowledge of past lives, of the divine eye, of the extinction of defilements) and the five conducts (holy, pure, heavenly, infant, and illness conduct); fifth, Well-Gone, freely and well departing, entering nirvāṇa; sixth, Understander of the World, able to understand all the affairs and principles of the world; seventh, Supreme Man, the man above all; eighth, Tamer of Men, the great man who can tame those who cultivate the right path; ninth, Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha is teacher of all gods and humans; tenth, Buddha World-Honored One, the Buddha is the one revered by all the world. “Secure” — peaceful and stable: a state of bliss and stability, not disturbed by any affliction. “Living beings” — also called sentient beings, that is, all creatures with consciousness.

blocks.text: (1) Why Is It Called Ultimate Bliss?

inline.s: “Moreover, Shariputra, for what cause, for what condition, is that Buddha-world called Ultimate Bliss? Shariputra, because in that world all classes of beings are free from all suffering and distress of body and mind, and have only measureless pure joy. Therefore it is called the world of Ultimate Bliss.”

“Shariputra, why is the world of the Buddha of Measureless Life called the world of Ultimate Bliss? Shariputra, because in that world the beings are free from all suffering and distress of body and mind, and have only measureless pure joy. Therefore this world is called the world of Ultimate Bliss.”

blocks.text: (2) The Adornments of the Retribution of the Environment

inline.s: “Retribution of the environment” — the retribution upon which sentient beings depend for their dwelling, such as the land, the earth, houses and utensils; that is, the conditions of life.

“Moreover, Shariputra, in the pure Buddha-land of the world of Ultimate Bliss, everywhere there are seven rows of marvellous jewel railings, seven rows of jeweled tala trees, and sevenfold marvellous jewel netting, surrounding it on all sides, adorned with four kinds of treasure: gold treasure, silver treasure, vaidurya treasure, and sphatika treasure, embellished in elegant interplay. Shariputra, in that Buddha-land there are ornaments of fine elegance such as these, adorned with virtue and merit, and greatly to be loved and delighted in. Therefore it is called the world of Ultimate Bliss.”

“Moreover, Shariputra, in the pure Buddha-land of the world of Ultimate Bliss, everywhere there are seven-tiered rows of marvellous jewel railings, seven-tiered rows of jeweled tala trees, and sevenfold marvellous jewel netting, surrounding it on all sides, adorned in criss-crossing and delightful ways with the four treasures of gold, silver, vaidurya and sphatika. Shariputra, in that Buddha-land there are
elegant adornments
such as these, together with glory of virtue and merit, greatly to be loved and delighted in. Therefore it is called the world of Ultimate Bliss.”
“Railing” — a balustrade. The horizontal bar is the “railing”; the upright post (shǔn/dùn) is the balustrade. “Marvellous treasure” — wondrous and precious jewels.
“Seven tiers of marvellous jewel railings, seven tiers of jeweled tala trees, and sevenfold marvellous jewel netting”
— the railings surround the trees, and the marvellous jewel netting covers the trees, one after another in layers, and their number is seven. The Sutra of the Buddha of Measureless Life says:

“Measureless jewel netting spreads over the Buddha-land, all woven of golden threads, true pearls and hundreds of thousands of mixed treasures, wondrous and rare, adorned and embellished, hanging down on all four sides with jeweled bells, their light and colors shining, altogether of surpassing splendor. Naturally the wind of virtue rises gently and stirs. The breeze is harmonious, neither cold nor hot, mild and soft, neither slow nor swift. It blows upon the netting and the many jeweled trees, and unfolds measureless and subtle sounds of the Dharma, spreading abroad ten thousand kinds of gentle and elegant virtue-fragrance. Those who hear it, their dusty toils and habitual defilements naturally do not arise. When the wind touches their bodies, they are all blissful, as when a bhikshu attains the samādhi of extinction.”
“Elegant adornments” — beautiful and ornate decoration. “Glory of virtue and merit” — the vast, magnificent and lovely merit.

blocks.text: 2. The Jeweled Pools and Water of Eight Qualities

inline.s: “Moreover, Shariputra, in the pure Buddha-land of the world of Ultimate Bliss, everywhere there are pools of seven marvellous treasures, filled with the water of the eight qualities. What are called the water of the eight qualities? First, clear; second, cold and refreshing; third, sweet and delicious; fourth, light and soft; fifth, moistening; sixth, peaceful and harmonious; seventh, when drunk, it removes hunger and thirst and countless other evils; eighth, when drunk, it certainly nourishes the various faculties and the four great elements, and increases all manner of supreme good roots. Beings of much merit constantly delight in enjoying it.”

“Moreover, Shariputra, in the pure Buddha-land of the world of Ultimate Bliss, everywhere there are pools of seven marvellous treasures, filled with the water of the eight qualities. Why is it called the water of the eight qualities? Because this water has eight virtues: first, clear; second, cold and refreshing; third, sweet and delicious; fourth, light and soft; fifth, moistening; sixth, peaceful and harmonious; seventh, when drunk, it removes hunger and thirst and countless other evils; eighth, when drunk, it certainly nourishes body and mind and increases all manner of supreme good roots. Beings of much merit constantly delight in enjoying it.”

“The various faculties and the four great elements” — this refers to body and mind. The “various faculties” are the six faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body and mind. The “four great elements” are earth, water, fire and wind. Earth has the nature of solidity, water of wetness, fire of warmth, wind of movement. All the tangible things of the world, including the body, possess the four natures of solid, wet, warm and moving, and so they are called “great.”

“In these jeweled pools the bottom is spread with golden sand, and on all four sides there are four stairways, adorned with the four treasures and greatly to be enjoyed. Around these pools there are marvellous jewel trees, set out in rows with elegant adornment, their fragrance rich and penetrating, adorned with the seven treasures and greatly to be enjoyed. What are called the seven treasures? First, gold; second, silver; third, vaidurya; fourth, sphatika; fifth, red pearls; sixth, ashmagarbha gems; seventh, musaragalva gems.”

“In these jeweled pools the bottom is spread over with golden sand; about them on four sides there are four stairways, all adorned with the four treasures of gold, silver, vaidurya and sphatika, greatly to be enjoyed. Around the pools of the seven treasures there are marvellous jewel trees of flowers, set out in rows with elegant adornment, their fragrance rich and penetrating, adorned with the seven treasures and greatly to be enjoyed. These seven treasures are: first, gold; second, silver; third, vaidurya; fourth, sphatika; fifth, red pearls; sixth, ashmagarbha gems; seventh, musaragalva gems.”

“In these pools there are always lotus flowers of many colors, as large as chariot wheels. Blue in form, blue in appearance, blue in light, blue in shadow; yellow in form, yellow in appearance, yellow in light, yellow in shadow; red in form, red in appearance, red in light, red in shadow; white in form, white in appearance, white in light, white in shadow; four forms, four appearances, four lights, four shadows. Shariputra, in that Buddha-land there are ornaments of fine elegance such as these, adorned with virtue and merit, and greatly to be loved and delighted in. Therefore it is called the world of Ultimate Bliss.”

“In these jeweled pools there are always lotus flowers of many different colors, as large as chariot wheels. The blue lotus shimmers with blue light, the yellow lotus shimmers with yellow light, the red lotus shimmers with red light, and the white lotus shimmers with white light; these four colors of lotus shimmer with blue, yellow, red and white lights. Shariputra, in that Buddha-land there are
elegant adornments
such as these, together with glory of virtue and merit, greatly to be loved and delighted in. Therefore it is called the world of Ultimate Bliss.”
“Fragrant (fēn fù)” — sweet-smelling. “Adorned” — a decoration of surpassing beauty. “Of many colors” — many colors.

“Moreover, Shariputra, in the pure Buddha-land of the world of Ultimate Bliss, there naturally resound countlessly many and boundless kinds of marvellous music, their tones harmonious and elegant, greatly to be loved and delighted in. When the classes of beings hear these wonderful sounds, all their evil afflictions are entirely extinguished, and countless wholesome dharmas gradually grow, until they swiftly attain the unexcelled, right and equal enlightenment. Shariputra, in that Buddha-land there are ornaments of fine elegance such as these, adorned with virtue and merit, and greatly to be loved and delighted in. Therefore it is called the world of Ultimate Bliss.”

“Moreover, Shariputra, in the pure Buddha-land of the world of Ultimate Bliss, there naturally always resounds countlessly much and boundless music, its melody harmonious and elegant, greatly to be loved and delighted in. All beings, hearing these wonderful sounds, have all their evil afflictions completely extinguished, and countless wholesome dharmas gradually grow, until they swiftly attain the fruit of Buddhahood.
Shariputra, in that Buddha-land there are
elegant adornments
such as these, together with glory of virtue and merit, greatly to be loved and delighted in. Therefore it is called the world of Ultimate Bliss.”
“Music (jì yuè)”
— musical sound.

“Unexcelled right and equal enlightenment” — that is, unexcelled right and equal enlightenment; “bodhi” is translated as “enlightenment.” “Unexcelled right and equal enlightenment” — the new translation of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi; it is the supreme wisdom that truly, equally and perfectly knows all truth, that is, the ultimate and perfect fruit of Buddhahood.

“Moreover, Shariputra, in the pure Buddha-land of the world of Ultimate Bliss, the whole of the earth is formed of pure gold, its touch soft, fragrant, clean and bright; marvellous treasures, measureless and boundless, adorn it in between. Shariputra, in that Buddha-land there are ornaments of fine elegance such as these, adorned with virtue and merit, and greatly to be loved and delighted in. Therefore it is called the world of Ultimate Bliss.”

“Moreover, Shariputra, in the pure Buddha-land of the world of Ultimate Bliss, the whole of the earth is formed of pure gold, its nature soft and yielding, fragrant, clean and bright, adorned amid and between with measureless and boundless marvellous treasures. Shariputra, in that Buddha-land there are
elegant adornments
such as these, together with glory of virtue and merit, greatly to be loved and delighted in. Therefore it is called the world of Ultimate Bliss.”

blocks.text: 7. The Perpetual Rain of Heavenly Flowers

inline.s: “Moreover, Shariputra, in the pure Buddha-land of the world of Ultimate Bliss, throughout the six periods of the day and night, there always rains every kind of supremely wondrous heavenly flower, glossy and fragrant, fine and soft, of many colors. Though it causes those who see it to be at ease and glad in body and mind, they do not cling to it, and it increases in beings measurelessly many, countless and inconceivable supreme merits.”

“Moreover, Shariputra, in the pure Buddha-land of the world of Ultimate Bliss, within the twenty-four hours of the day and night, there constantly rain down from the sky all manner of exceedingly beautiful heavenly flowers. These heavenly flowers are glossy and fragrant, fine and soft, of every color, and although they cause those who see them to be at ease and glad in body and mind, yet one does not cling to them, and they increase in beings measurelessly many, countless and inconceivable supreme merits.”

“Those classes of beings, throughout the six periods of the day and night, constantly hold these flowers to make offerings to the Buddha of Measureless Life. Each morning they take these heavenly flowers and, within the space of a mealtime, fly to the measureless worlds of other directions and make offerings to hundreds of thousands of crores of Buddhas. At the place of each Buddha, they take hundreds of thousands of crores of flowers and scatter them as an offering. Then they return to their own place and roam, abide in the heavenly dwellings, and the like.”

“The beings there, throughout the twenty-four hours of the day and night, constantly hold these heavenly flowers to make offerings to the Buddha of Measureless Life. Each morning they take these heavenly flowers and, within the space of a single meal, fly to the measureless worlds of other directions to make offerings to hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas. At the place of each Buddha they take hundreds of thousands of millions of flowers and scatter them in offering. Then they return to their own place and walk, abide in meditative calm, and so on.”

“The six periods” — the three periods of day and the three periods of night, together called the six periods. The three periods of day are morning, noon, and evening; the three periods of night are the first, middle and last watches. In ancient India one period equaled four hours of the present age, and six periods totaled twenty-four hours. “The Buddha of Measureless Life” — that is, Amitābha Buddha, the lord of the Land of Ultimate Bliss in the west. “Amita” is the transliteration and “measureless life” the translation. “Roam, abide in the heavenly dwellings, and so on” — to walk (cankrama), and to meditate (abiding in the divine). The Master Xuanzang's Abhidharma-samayapradipika (chapter six) says: “What is the divine abiding? Answer: the four dhyanas. What are the four? That is, having discarded desire and unwholesome dharmas, with thought and deliberation, born of separation there is joy and bliss, and one enters the first dhyana and dwells in it completely; and so on, up to entering the fourth dhyana and dwelling in it completely. As the Blessed One said to the brahmin Venapulla: ‘Brahmin, know this: at that time when I, for the sake of any one of the four dhyanas in the world, go forth, then I go forth for the sake of the divine abiding; at that time when I, for the sake of any one of the four dhyanas, abide or sit or lie down, then I abide or sit or lie down for the sake of the divine abiding.’ Thus, among the four dhyanas of the world, having drawn near to any one dhyana and repeatedly studied it, earnestly and unremittingly and without abandoning cultivating it, this is called the divine abiding.” The separate translation of the Miscellaneous Agama Sutra (chapter two) says: “At that time, when the morning came, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl, entered the city to beg for food. Having eaten, he washed his feet, gathered his seat, went to the Grove of the Clear Eye, and after surveying it, sat with crossed legs at a quiet place beneath a tree, abiding in the divine abiding.” “Meditative calm (dhyana)” — to sit in quiet thought, that is, meditative concentration.

“Shariputra, in that Buddha-land there are ornaments of fine elegance such as these, adorned with virtue and merit, and greatly to be loved and delighted in. Therefore it is called the world of Ultimate Bliss.”
Shariputra, in that Buddha-land there are
elegant adornments
such as these, together with glory of virtue and merit, greatly to be loved and delighted in. Therefore it is called the world of Ultimate Bliss.”

blocks.text: 8. The Multitude of Birds Preach the Dharma

inline.s: “Moreover, Shariputra, in the pure Buddha-land of the world of Ultimate Bliss, there are always all kinds of marvellous, lovely, many-colored flocks of birds — such as geese, wild-geese, herons, egrets, wild swans, cranes, peacocks, parrots, kalavinkas, and the jivamjivaka and the like. These flocks of birds, throughout the six periods of the day and night, constantly gather together and utter harmonious and elegant sounds. According to the voice of their kind, they proclaim the wonderful Dharma, namely the profound mindfulness, right efforts, psychic powers, faculties, powers, and limbs of enlightenment, and the path — countless wonderful dharmas.”

“Moreover, Shariputra, in the pure Buddha-land of the world of Ultimate Bliss, there are always all kinds of marvellous, lovely and gorgeously colored flocks of birds — geese, wild-geese, herons, egrets, wild swans, cranes, peacocks, parrots, kalavinkas, jivamjivaka and the like. These flocks of birds, throughout the twenty-four hours of the day and night, always gather together and sound harmonious and elegant voices. According to the sound of their kind, they proclaim the wonderful Dharma: that is, the profound four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four psychic powers, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven limbs of enlightenment, and the eightfold path — countless wonderful dharmas.”

“Heron (qiū)” — a water bird with no feathers on head and neck. “Egrets (lù)” — a bird with great wings and a short tail, a straight pointed beak, and very long neck and legs; the common ones are the “white egret,” the “gray heron,” the “green heron” and so on. “Wild swan” — a large goose. “Crane” — the divine crane. “Kalavinka” — that is, kalavinka (the sweet-voiced bird). “Jivamjivaka” — that is, the life-life bird (a bird with one body and two heads).

“Mindfulness, right efforts, psychic powers, faculties, powers, limbs of enlightenment and path” — these are among the thirty-seven aids to enlightenment: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four psychic powers, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven limbs of enlightenment, and the eightfold path. Their correspondences are: mindfulness (the four foundations of mindfulness), right efforts (the four right efforts), psychic powers (the four psychic powers), faculties (the five faculties), powers (the five powers), limbs of enlightenment and path (the seven limbs of enlightenment and the eightfold path). “Right efforts” — that is, “right diligence.” The Treasury of Abhidharma (book twenty-five) says: “Why is diligence called right cutting off? Because in the stage of the right practice of cutting off defilements, this diligence has the power to cut off indolence.” “Psychic powers” — that is, the four psychic powers, also named the four wishful powers; they are originally four kinds of meditative concentration, such that one who cultivates them can develop psychic powers as he wishes. First, the wishful power of desire — the increase of the desire to practice the Way and attain the fruit; second, the wishful power of mind — with single thought after single thought, abiding in right principle; third, the wishful power of effort — advancing with vigor and without interruption of merit; fourth, the wishful power of wisdom — true illumination, free from error, the mind not scattered. “Limbs of enlightenment and path” — the seven limbs of enlightenment (also called the seven factors of enlightenment) and the eightfold path (also called the noble eightfold path). “The thirty-seven aids to enlightenment” — the thirty-seven methods of practice upon the path of enlightenment; cultivating them in order, one may gradually proceed toward enlightenment.

“The beings of that land, having heard these sounds, each attain the countless merits of mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, and mindfulness of the Sangha, and are steadily cultivated by them. You, Shariputra, what do you think? Are the flocks of birds of that land of the class of the wretched animals, the evil destinies? Do not hold such a view! Why? Because in that Buddha's pure land there are no three evil destinies; one does not even hear the name of the three evil destinies, how much less their reality — the birds as creatures born of evil karma. Know that they are all transformations wrought by the Buddha of Measureless Life, causing them to proclaim the measureless sound of the Dharma and to bring benefit and bliss to beings.”

“The beings of that land, having heard these sounds, each attain the measureless merits of mindfulness of the Buddha, of the Dharma and of the Sangha, and are steadily cultivated by them. Shariputra, what do you think of this? Are the flocks of birds there the animals of the evil destinies? Do not think so! Why? Because the pure Buddha-land of the Buddha of Measureless Life has no three evil destinies of hell, hungry ghosts and animals; one does not even hear the names of the three evil destinies, how much less the flocks of animals born of evil karma. You should know that all of these are transformations wrought by the Buddha of Measureless Life through the power of Dharma, causing them to proclaim and spread the measureless sound of the Dharma, and to bring benefit and bliss to all beings.”

“Beasts (páng shēng)” — also written páng shēng, that is, animals; “páng” means crooked, by which is meant that because they acted crookedly, they are born through a crooked birth. “Evil destinies” — evil courses. “Are the flocks of birds of that land of the class of the beasts of evil destinies?” — these birds of the Land of Ultimate Bliss — could they be beings of the evil destinies? “Know that they are all transformations wrought by the Buddha of Measureless Life” — know that all these birds are transformations wrought by Amitābha Buddha through the power of Dharma. Judged by modern science and technology, these birds are all intelligent machine-birds devoid of consciousness (just as intelligent robots). Of course, as science and technology develop, holographic birds could likewise achieve the same effect. “Proclaim and spread” — to proclaim and propagate.

blocks.text: 9. The Marvellous Wind Preaches the Dharma

inline.s: “Moreover, Shariputra, in the pure Buddha-land of the world of Ultimate Bliss, there is always a marvellous wind blowing upon the jeweled trees and the jeweled netting, producing subtle sounds. It is as when hundreds of thousands of crores of heavenly music are at once played, emitting subtle sounds greatly to be enjoyed. Just so in that land, there is always a marvellous wind blowing upon the many jeweled trees and the jeweled netting, striking them into all kinds of subtle sounds that speak of various dharmas. When the beings of that land hear these sounds, the mindfulness of the Buddha, the Dharma and the Sangha, and attention, arise, with countless merits.”

“Moreover, Shariputra, in the pure Buddha-land of the world of Ultimate Bliss, there is always a marvellous breeze gently blowing upon the jeweled trees and the jeweled netting, producing subtle sounds. It is just as when hundreds of thousands of millions of heavenly musics sound all at once, emitting subtle sounds greatly to be loved and savored. These subtle sounds speak of all manner of dharmas. When the beings of that land hear these sounds, the mindfulness of the Buddha, of the Dharma and of the Sangha, and right attention arise in them, and they attain countless merits.”
“To savor” — to ponder and realize over and over. “Attention” — to concentrate one's spirit and keep the mind alert.

“Moreover, Shariputra, in the pure Buddha-land of the world of Ultimate Bliss, there are things measureless and boundless, inconceivable and supremely rare, such as these. Even if, for hundreds of thousands of crores of nayutas of eons, with its measureless hundreds of thousands of crores of nayutas of tongues, and each tongue emitting a measureless sound, one were to praise its merits, still one could not exhaust them. Therefore it is called the world of Ultimate Bliss.”

“Shariputra, in the pure Buddha-land of the world of Ultimate Bliss, there are things measureless and boundless, inconceivable and supremely rare, such as these. Even if, for hundreds of thousands of millions of eons, with measureless hundreds of thousands of millions of tongues, each tongue emitting a measureless sound, one were to praise their merits, still one could not exhaust them. Therefore it is called the world of Ultimate Bliss.”

blocks.text: (3) The Adornments of the Proper Retribution

inline.s: “Proper retribution” — the body and mind of the Buddha and of sentient beings; this is the substance of the retribution drawn to oneself through past karma.

“Moreover, Shariputra, in the pure Buddha-land of the world of Ultimate Bliss, for what cause is the Buddha named Measureless Life? Shariputra, because that Tathagata and all the beings there have a lifespan of measureless and countless great eons. For this reason the Tathagata of that land is named Measureless Life. Shariputra, the Buddha of Measureless Life, since he attained anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, has passed ten great eons.”

“Then, Shariputra, the Buddha of the pure Buddha-land of the world of Ultimate Bliss — for what cause is he named Measureless Life? Shariputra, this is because the Buddha and all the beings there have a lifespan of measureless and countless great eons. For this reason the Buddha there is named Measureless Life. Shariputra, the Buddha of Measureless Life, since his attainment of Buddhahood, has already passed ten great eons.”

“Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi” — the name of Buddha-wisdom, translated into Chinese as “unexcelled right and equal enlightenment,” which is the supreme wisdom that truly, equally and perfectly knows all truth.

“Shariputra, for what cause is that Buddha named Measureless Light? Shariputra, because that Tathagata ever radiates measureless and boundless wonderful Light, illumining all the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, doing the work of the Buddha without obstruction. For this reason the Tathagata of that land is named Measureless Light. Shariputra, that Buddha's pure land is accomplished with such glory of merit and virtue, greatly to be loved and delighted in. Therefore it is called the world of Ultimate Bliss.”

Śāriputra, for what reason is the Buddha there also called Immeasurable Light? Śāriputra, it is because this Tathāgata unceasingly emits an immeasurable, boundless, wondrous radiance that illumines all the Buddha-lands in the ten directions and carries on the Buddha-work without any obstruction. For this reason, that Tathāgata there is also called Immeasurable Light. Śāriputra, that Buddha's Pure Land is endowed with such merits and adornments that it is utterly delightful and pleasing. Therefore it is called the Land of Ultimate Bliss.”

“Moreover, Śāriputra, in the purified Buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, Amitāyus Buddha constantly has immeasurable śrāvaka disciples, all of whom are great arhats, endowed with all manner of subtle merits, boundless in number and beyond all reckoning. Śāriputra, that Buddha's Pure Land is adorned with such merits and splendors that it is utterly delightful and pleasing. Therefore it is called the Land of Ultimate Bliss.”

And, Śāriputra, in the purified Buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, Amitāyus Buddha constantly has immeasurable śrāvaka disciples, all of whom are great arhats, endowed with all manner of subtle merits, boundless in number and beyond all reckoning. Śāriputra, that Buddha's Pure Land is adorned with such merits and splendors that it is utterly delightful and pleasing. Therefore it is called the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

“Moreover, Śāriputra, in the purified Buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, Amitāyus Buddha constantly has immeasurable bodhisattva disciples, all of whom are destined for a single more rebirth, endowed with all manner of subtle merits, boundless in number and beyond all reckoning. Even if one were to praise their merits for countless eons, one could never exhaust them. Śāriputra, that Buddha-land is adorned with such merits and splendors that it is utterly delightful and pleasing. Therefore it is called the Land of Ultimate Bliss.”

And, Śāriputra, in the purified Buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, Amitāyus Buddha has immeasurable bodhisattva disciples as well, all of whom are bodhisattvas of one more life, endowed with all manner of subtle merits, boundless in number and beyond all reckoning. Even if one were to praise their merits for countless great eons, one could never exhaust them. Śāriputra, that Buddha's Pure Land is adorned with such merits and splendors that it is utterly delightful and pleasing. Therefore it is called the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

[All are bound for a single more life]All these bodhisattva disciples are bodhisattvas bound for a single more life. [A bodhisattva bound for a single more life]That is, a bodhisattva who shall complete this one life to attain the Buddha-position.
[One more rebirth]With this single life, one is able to fill the Buddha's seat, a designation for a bodhisattva in the final body (an atavistic bodhisattva)

[The atavistic bodhisattva]The fifty-first of the fifty-two stages, the bodhisattva about to realize Buddhahood, whose merit and wisdom are nearly equal to a Buddha's; hence it is called “atavistic.” For instance, Avalokiteshvara, Mahasthamaprapta, and Maitreya are all atavistic bodhisattvas. [The fifty-two stages]From an ordinary being to Buddhahood, a bodhisattva passes through fifty-two stages: the ten faiths, the ten abodes, the ten practices, the ten dedications, the ten grounds, the atavistic, and the wondrous. [The wondrous]Self-enlightened and enlightening others, with enlightenment and practice both complete and wisdom and virtue inconceivable, it is called the “wondrous,” the unsurpassed right enlightenment of Buddhahood; one who realizes it is called a “Buddha.”

Question: Once sentient beings are reborn in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, they are free of birth and death and attain Buddhahood in a single life. Why, then, does it say here that a bodhisattva bound for a single more life is “one who fills the Buddha's seat in this one life”?

Answer: Birth and death are of two kinds: segmental birth-and-death and transforming birth-and-death. When it is said that “sentient beings reborn in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss are free of birth and death and attain Buddhahood in a single life,” the phrase “a single life” refers to a single life within segmental birth-and-death; whereas when it says “a bodhisattva bound for a single more life is one who fills the Buddha's seat in this one life,” the phrase “this one life” refers to a single life within transforming birth-and-death.

[Segmental birth-and-death]For sentient beings within the three realms and six destinies, owing to the karmic ripening of good and evil deeds, their lifespans have limits and their bodies have distinctions, hence their birth-and-death is called “segmental birth-and-death.” One who ends segmental birth-and-death escapes the cycle and leaves the three realms. [Transforming birth-and-death]The sages of the three vehicles (the śrāvaka vehicle, the pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the bodhisattva vehicle), having already cut off the delusions of views and thoughts and ended segmental birth-and-death, in the course of practice see delusion gradually extinguished and realization gradually increased; each period of this migration from delusion to awakening differs, and the passage from one period to the next is like a single birth-and-death, its transformation mysterious and inconceivable; hence it is named “transforming birth-and-death.” One who ends transforming birth-and-death fully realizes the Buddha-fruit.

“Moreover, Śāriputra, all sentient beings reborn in that land never regress; they will never again fall into the dangerous evil destinies, the borderlands, or the lowly, contemptible barbarous states. They forever roam the pure lands of the Buddhas, and their supreme vows and practices increase with every thought, so that they are certain to realize anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. Śāriputra, that Buddha-land is adorned with such merits and splendors that it is utterly delightful and pleasing. Therefore it is called the Land of Ultimate Bliss.”

And, Śāriputra, all sentient beings reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss never regress; they will certainly never again fall into the evil destinies, the borderlands, or the lowly castes. They forever roam the pure lands of the Buddhas, and their supreme vows and practices increase with every thought, so that they are certain to realize the Buddha-fruit. Śāriputra, that Buddha's Pure Land is endowed with such merits and splendors that it is utterly delightful and pleasing. Therefore it is called the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

[Mleccha]A lowly, contemptible caste. The Huayan Commentary says: “Mleccha, as the Tripitaka master says, means ‘the worst of the wicked,’ also called ‘the lowest of the lowly’ — these are free renderings of its meaning.”
Question: Are there women in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss?
Answer: There are no women in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss. In the Sutra of the Buddha Speaks of the Amitābha Buddha, the Buddha made this vow while still on the causal ground:

“My second vow: when I become a Buddha, may there be no women in my land. Women who wish to be reborn in my land shall all be transformed into men. The countless gods and humans, and all winged, crawling, and swimming creatures, on being reborn in my land, shall all be born by transformation in the lotus flowers of the seven-jeweled pools. Grown, they shall all become bodhisattvas and arhats, without any limit of number. Only when this vow is fulfilled shall I become a Buddha; if it is not fulfilled, I shall never become a Buddha.”
The Sutra of the Buddha Speaks of the Immeasurable Pure and Equal Enlightenment says:

“In that land are all bodhisattvas and arhats, without any women, of extremely long life, with lifespans that likewise stretch over countless eons. Women who are reborn there are transformed and all become men.”
Bodhisattva Vasubandhu's Treatise on Rebirth says:

“The land of Mahāyāna good roots is free alike of all reproachful names; women and those with deficient faculties, and the two-vehicle seeds, are not born there; whatever sentient beings delight in, all of it is fulfilled.”
Master Yinguang says:
“In the Land of Ultimate Bliss there are no women. Women, and even animals, reborn in that world all appear in the form of young boys, born by transformation in lotus flowers.”
（From Master Yinguang's Collected Writings, Third Compilation
Reply to Mr. Ye Fubei, Letter One）
[Wú yāng]Without limit, inexhaustible.

“Moreover, Śāriputra, if any sentient being hears of the immeasurable merits and manifold adornments that adorn the pure Buddha-land of Amitāyus Buddha in the West, they should all make the vow to be reborn in that Buddha-land. Why is that? Because if they are reborn there, they will be gathered together in one assembly with those great beings adorned with such immeasurable merits, and will enjoy the Dharma-bliss of the Great Vehicle in that pure Buddha-land of immeasurable merits and manifold adornments, never regressing, with their immeasurable vows and practices increasing with every thought, swiftly realizing the unsurpassed right and equal enlightenment.”

Therefore, Śāriputra, if any sentient being hears of the immeasurable merits and manifold adornments of the pure Buddha-land of Amitāyus Buddha in the West, they should all make the vow to be reborn in that Buddha-land. Why is that? Because if they are reborn there, they will be gathered together in one assembly with those great bodhisattvas who are endowed with such immeasurable merits and manifold adornments, and will enjoy the Dharma-bliss of the Great Vehicle in that pure Buddha-land of immeasurable merits and manifold adornments, never regressing, with their immeasurable vows and practices increasing with every thought, swiftly realizing the Buddha-fruit.

“Śāriputra, the sentient beings reborn in that Buddha-land all accomplish immeasurable and boundless merits. Those sentient beings of little good root are not able to be reborn in the pure Buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitāyus Buddha.”
Śāriputra, all sentient beings reborn in that Buddha-land accomplish immeasurable and boundless merits. Those sentient beings whose good roots
（the goodness of the three karmas of body, speech, and mind）
are small cannot be reborn in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss.

[Good roots]That is, the goodness of the three karmas of body, speech, and mind; because it can give rise to wondrous fruit, it is called good root. [The goodness of the three karmas of body, speech, and mind]Not killing, not stealing, not committing sexual misconduct — this is the goodness of the body; not lying, not speaking divisively, not speaking harshly, not speaking frivolously — this is the goodness of speech; not greed, not anger, not delusion — this is the goodness of mind.
[Sentient beings]Also called living beings, all animals endowed with consciousness and feeling.
In the Contemplation Sutra of Immeasurable Life, the Buddha says:
“Those who wish to be born in that land
（the Western World of Ultimate Bliss）

should cultivate the three kinds of merit: first, being filial to and supporting one's parents, serving teachers and elders, being compassionate and not killing, and cultivating the ten wholesome deeds; second, taking refuge in the Three Jewels, observing all the precepts, and never violating the rules of conduct; third, arousing the bodhi mind, deeply believing in cause and effect, reciting the Mahāyāna scriptures, and encouraging fellow practitioners.”
Therefore, those who recite the Buddha's name must earnestly cultivate the three kinds of merit of the pure karma, so as to be endowed with the conditions of many good roots and merits.

[The ten wholesome deeds]Ten kinds of wholesome karma: not killing, not stealing, not committing sexual misconduct, not lying, not speaking divisively (not sowing discord), not speaking harshly (not uttering cutting or cruel words), not speaking frivolously (not saying meaningless words), not greed, not anger, not delusion (not going against principle). See in detail
The Annotated Sutra of the Ten Wholesome Karmic Paths

. [The three refuges]That is, the three refuges: taking refuge in the Buddha, taking refuge in the Dharma, taking refuge in the Sangha. This is taking refuge in the Three Jewels: all Buddhas are the Buddha-jewel, the right Dharma is the Dharma-jewel, and the noble Sangha is the Sangha-jewel. [Arousing the bodhi mind]Arousing the great mind that seeks Buddhahood above (attaining enlightenment) and delivers sentient beings below.
The Buddha-Dharma has the three studies of precepts, concentration, and wisdom; precepts are the foundation of concentration,
so those who recite the Buddha's name must strictly observe the five precepts and the ten wholesome deeds to increase their good roots and merits

, and lay a solid foundation. If one lacks good roots and merits, one is constantly bewitched by the objects of the senses and entangled by karmic hindrances, so that single-minded recollection can hardly be accomplished. Therefore, before teaching about single-minded, unconfused recollection, the Buddha especially pointed out:
“Sentient beings of little good root are not able to be reborn in the pure Buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitāyus Buddha.”
In the Sutra of the Buddha Speaks of Immeasurable Life, the Buddha says:

“One should resolve oneself, keep the body upright and act rightly, and all the more do all manner of good. Cultivate oneself and purify the body, washing away the defilements of the mind. Let one's words be faithful and one's conduct sincere, outer and inner in accord. One who can save oneself and in turn rescue others, earnestly seeking the vow,
accumulates the root of good
. Though one labors diligently for a single life, in a moment one is reborn in the land of Immeasurable Life, with bliss without end.”

[The five precepts]Not killing, not stealing, not committing sexual misconduct, not lying, not drinking alcohol. Not killing is not taking the life of living creatures; not stealing is not taking the property of others; not committing sexual misconduct is not engaging in sexual acts outside the marriage bond; not lying is not speaking deceitful, misleading words; not drinking alcohol is not taking intoxicating liquors or drugs that stupefy the mind.

Therefore, while earnestly reciting the Buddha's name（the right practice）, one must also cut off evil and cultivate good（the assisting practice）, so as to clear away the hindrances on the path of progress.
Master Yinguang says:

“Recite the Buddha's name with single mind and, at the same time, cultivate worldly good as a supporting practice, following the method of the Great Masters Yongming and Lianchi, and there is nothing that will not succeed. Reform your own evil and cultivate good, and recite the Buddha's name with single mind. All relatives, old friends, and those with whom you have ties should likewise be taught in this way.”
（From Reply to a Certain Layman of Yongjia, Letter Six）He further says:

“As to the method of cultivation, only recitation of the name is foremost, and so one should concentrate chiefly on faith, vows, and recitation of the name. Then, taking ‘commit no evil, practice all good’ as the supporting practice, the benefit is great indeed.”
（From Reply to Layman Fang Shengzhao, Letter Six）
