[Cultivating good]To do charitable deeds is indeed cultivating good, but the most essential cultivation of good is still the goodness of one's own three karmas of body, speech, and mind（
not killing, not stealing, not committing sexual misconduct, not lying, not speaking divisively, not speaking harshly, not speaking frivolously, not greed, not anger, not delusion

）. Therefore, cultivating good chiefly means cultivating the goodness of one's own three karmas of body, speech, and mind. The Great Master Shandao, who was an emanation of Amitābha Buddha, has set us a shining example:
“He guarded the precepts so strictly that he did not violate the slightest rule.”

（See in detail The Records of the Pure Land Sages and Worthies）It is regrettable that nowadays some teachings vaguely lump together the cutting off of evil and the cultivation of good as “miscellaneous practices,” setting precepts in opposition to reciting the Buddha's name, and even loudly proclaiming: there is no need to cut off evil or cultivate good, it does not matter to commit evil for a whole lifetime, because the evil person is the very right object of Amitābha Buddha's deliverance.（See in detail
The Primal Vow Dharma-Gate Is a Deviant Teaching Attached to Buddhism
）[Precept-conduct]The conduct of strictly observing the precepts.
In
the course schedule of the Online Buddhist Academy of Cultivating According to the Teaching
‘s “Pure Practice”

, the first stage is “cutting off evil and cultivating good.” Through the study of this stage, one comes to understand the principles, methods, and practical steps of cutting off evil and cultivating good, enabling one to do so more systematically, more deeply, and more solidly.

At the same time, one should also cultivate the four immeasurable minds of friendliness, compassion, joy, and equanimity, and apply them in daily life, so as to remove suffering and give joy, without resentment or distress, without anger or hatred.

[The four immeasurable minds]The mind of unlimited friendliness, the mind of unlimited compassion, the mind of unlimited joy, and the mind of unlimited equanimity. Giving happiness to all sentient beings is called the “mind of unlimited friendliness”; removing the suffering of all sentient beings is called the “mind of unlimited compassion”; seeing others do good, or be freed from suffering and attain happiness, and giving rise to deep joy is called the “mind of unlimited joy”; letting go of the above three minds without attachment, treating friend and foe alike, without arousing love or hate, is called the “mind of unlimited equanimity.” Because these four minds are directed to immeasurable sentient beings and give rise to immeasurable blessings, they are called “immeasurable minds.”
Question: I too well know that cutting off evil and cultivating good is the foundation of pure-land practice, but I feel it is hard to begin. What should I do?
Answer: Concerning how to begin cutting off evil and cultivating good, I especially recommend to you a short piece:
The Record of Mr. Yu Jingyi Meeting the God of the Kitchen (Original Text and Colloquial Version)
（its annotations are is in
The Annotated Record of Mr. Yu Jingyi Meeting the God of the Kitchen

）— this is an exemplar of transforming one's destiny. I hope you read it repeatedly, ponder and savor it, and put it into practice. The stage of putting it into practice is especially important; only through continuous practice can one grasp the true meaning of the piece; and moreover, repeated reading and pondering and savoring are all for the sake of putting it into practice. If time permits, it would be best to follow
the course schedule of the Online Buddhist Academy of Cultivating According to the Teaching
‘s “Pure Practice”
, and systematically study the five courses of the first stage, “cutting off evil and cultivating good.” Likewise, in this course of study the emphasis remains on putting it into practice.
It must be pointed out that the World-Honored One especially emphasized in the sutras:
“Sentient beings of little good root are not able to be reborn in the pure Buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitāyus Buddha.”

Yet the primal vow Dharma-gate loudly proclaims: to be reborn in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss “one need not cut off evil or cultivate good,” “one need not observe the precepts,” “committing evil and crime is of no consequence,” “the evil person is the very right object of Amitābha Buddha's deliverance,” and “reciting the name guarantees rebirth,” and so on（see in detail
The Primal Vow Dharma-Gate Is a Deviant Teaching Attached to Buddhism

）. This is virtually leading people into a pit of fire, overturning the Buddha's teaching in direct opposition to him. The believers beguiled by them neither earnestly recite the Buddha's name（they could well have done so, but because of the deception they thought “reciting the name guarantees rebirth” and so grew careless and did not earnestly recite）, nor cut off evil and cultivate good and observe the ten wholesome deeds, and even, relying on the assurance that “the evil person is the very right object of Amitābha Buddha's deliverance,” give free rein to evil. As a result, not only are they not reborn in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, but when their life ends, dragged along by their evil karma, they fall into the three evil realms（hell, hungry ghosts, and beasts）, unable even to preserve a human body.

The functions of cutting off evil and cultivating good and observing precepts are: first, to tame the mind; second, to increase merit and virtue; third, to eradicate karmic hindrances. If those who recite the Buddha's name do not cut off evil and cultivate good and do not observe the precepts, their minds are like a wild horse or a mad elephant — how can they concentrate the mind on one object and attain single-minded, unconfused recitation? Merit and virtue are an aid on the bodhi path, while karmic hindrances are an obstruction on it. When merit and virtue (the aid) exceed karmic hindrances (the obstruction), one desires to do what should be done and does it energetically and with enjoyment; and what should not be done, one does not do, able to let it go decisively; at the end of life, the star of good fortune shines brightly, helping toward rebirth. When karmic hindrances (the obstruction) exceed merit and virtue (the aid), what should be done one does not want to do; even if one forces oneself, it is listless, doing little and stopping much; what should not be done one does energetically and with enjoyment, tirelessly; at the end of life, karmic hindrances appear and block rebirth.

For example, knowing well that “ten recitations at the end of life, sustained, bring about rebirth,” the most important first concern of one who recites the Buddha's name is to sustain the ten recitations at all times and places, so as to form a steady habit and nature. Therefore, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying, throughout the whole day, one should never let go of the sustained ten recitations; this is the great bliss and great liberation Dharma-gate for the wise. Yet many who recite the Buddha's name are unable to do so. In fact, “throughout the whole day, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying, never letting go of the sustained ten recitations” is not harder than going to work, and rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss surpasses being a billionaire beyond any measure beyond measure! Why is it that they cannot “never let go of the sustained ten recitations,” yet for a trifling profit can endure every kind of hardship and toil night and day? The reason is that they are obstructed by karma（if you analyze yourself and observe others, you will see just how karma hinders）. So the Buddha here specially taught:
“One cannot be reborn in that land by means of little good roots, merits, and conditions.”

“Moreover, Śāriputra, if there be a good man or good woman of pure faith who hears of the immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable meritorious name of Amitāyus Buddha and the merits and adornments of the Land of Ultimate Bliss,
and after hearing, reflects upon it
. If for one day and night, or two, or three, or four, or five, or six, or seven days and nights,
his recollection is single-minded and unconfused

. Then that good man or good woman, at the end of life, will find Amitāyus Buddha together with his immeasurable śrāvaka disciples and bodhisattvas, surrounding him front and behind, coming to stand before him, with compassion and aid, keeping his mind unconfused. Once he has relinquished his life, he follows the Buddha's assembly and is reborn in the pure Buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Immeasurable Life.”

Śāriputra, if there be a good man or good woman of pure faith who hears of the immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable meritorious name of Amitābha Buddha (Amitāyus Buddha) and the merits and adornments of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, then, having heard, binds the mind to reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha. If for one day and night, or two, or three, or four, or five, or six, or seven days and nights, he attains single-minded, unconfused recollection, then that good man or good woman, at the end of life, will find Amitābha Buddha together with his immeasurable śrāvaka disciples and bodhisattvas, surrounding him front and behind, coming to stand before him, with compassion and aid, keeping his mind unconfused. When life ends, he follows the Buddha and the assembly of sages and is reborn in the pure Buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Immeasurable Life.

[Good man]The Buddha calls a man who observes the five precepts and ten wholesome deeds a good man. [Good woman]The Buddha calls a woman who observes the five precepts and ten wholesome deeds a good woman.
[Reflect upon]To reflect upon the Buddha's name, that is,
to recite Amitābha Buddha
. The Sutra of the Fundamental Vows of the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha says:
At that time, the Tathāgata Flower of Enlightenment, Samādhi, Sovereign, and Free told the noble lady: when you have finished your offerings, only hasten back to your home, sit upright and
reflect upon my name

, and you shall know the place to which your mother has gone. At that time, the brahmin lady, having bowed to the Buddha, returned to her home. Because she was mindful of her mother, she sat upright and
recited the Tathāgata Flower of Enlightenment, Samādhi, Sovereign, and Free

[Single-minded, unconfused recollection]Binding the mind to reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha, clearly and distinctly, without drowsiness or distraction. [Following the Buddha's assembly]Following Amitābha Buddha (Amitāyus Buddha) and his immeasurable śrāvaka disciples and bodhisattvas.

Question: Since “that good man or good woman” has already attained single-minded, unconfused recollection, why does it say that after Amitāyus Buddha arrives, he “with compassion and aid, keeps his mind unconfused”?

Answer: Single-minded, unconfused recollection is what induces the Buddha's welcome, but it is a shallow level of skill, often insufficient to keep the mind unconfused when the four elements dissolve and the sufferings of the demonic states appear. Hence Amitāyus Buddha “with compassion and aid, keeps his mind unconfused,” so as to ensure rebirth in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss.
The Sutra of Praising the Merits of All the Buddhas says:
“When life is about to end, if one has single-minded faith and joy, mindful without abandoning
this is the right thought at the end of life, which induces the Buddha's welcome
, Amitābha Buddha will
（lead）
the assembly of monks
（the śrāvaka disciples and bodhisattvas）
and stand before him; the demons can never destroy the
（this good man or good woman）
mind of right enlightenment.”
Here, “the demons can never destroy the mind of right enlightenment” is precisely because Amitābha Buddha “with compassion and aid keeps his mind unconfused.”
Question: How does one engage in single-minded recollection?

Answer: As a traveler far from home recalls his native village and longs for his loving mother, so one recites the name. (Here “recall” means to think of with longing.) Master Yinguang's Praise of Bodhisattva Mahasthamaprapta says:
“As a child recalls its mother, so one recalls the World-Honored One
（Amitābha Buddha）
—immediately one receives his grace. The mind of the cause and the fruit of enlightenment both accord, and at once one returns to the source; gathering in the six senses is wondrous beyond words.”
The Śūraṅgama Sutra, Chapter on the Perfect Penetration of Bodhisattva Mahasthamaprapta through Buddha-Recitation, says:

“The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, in pity and remembrance of sentient beings, are like a mother recalling her child. If the child runs away, what use is the recall? But if the child recalls its mother in the same way the mother recalls the child, then, from life to life, mother and child are never far apart. If sentient beings are mindful of the Buddha and recite the Buddha, they will, in the present or in the future, certainly see the Buddha, never far from him. Without recourse to expedients, the mind is spontaneously opened. Like one who perfumes himself with incense, the body bears the fragrance. This is called the ornament of incense and light.”
（The annotations are in this study site
The Annotated Chapter on the Perfect Penetration of Bodhisattva Mahasthamaprapta through Buddha-Recitation
Question: Does the “clearly and distinctly” mentioned above mean that the Buddha's name must be recited with perfect clarity?

Answer: That is not the meaning. “Clearly and distinctly” means: the Buddha-name being recited should be clear and distinct in the mind (each phrase of the Buddha-name is clearly and distinctly known in the mind).
Question: What does “without drowsiness or distraction” mean?

Answer: “Without drowsiness or distraction” means: neither dull nor scattered. That is to say: if idle thoughts arise, know them but do not follow them, and do not be disturbed by them. Therefore, single-minded, unconfused recitation of the Buddha's name does not mean that not a single idle thought arises, but rather that one is not beguiled by idle thoughts and does not let them continue into thinking. On the whole, it means not being disturbed by idle thoughts. Of course, this is only the most elementary requirement of single-minded recollection; advancing further on this basis, one will reach the state in which thought after thought is free of idle thoughts and the Buddha-name is one pure mass.

Question: The sutra says: “If for one day and night, or two, or three, or four, or five, or six, or seven days and nights, his recollection is single-minded and unconfused.” Within one day and night, even up to seven days and nights, can one truly attain single-minded, unconfused recollection?

Answer: “One day and night even up to seven days and nights” is an illustrative expression, an abbreviated way of speech. The full statement, for example, is what the World-Honored One says in the Great Mindfulness-Sustaining Sutra:
“Bhikkhus! Anyone who rightly cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness in this way for
seven years
may expect one of two kinds of fruit: the highest wisdom in this very life
（realizing the fruit of arhatship）
, or, if the five aggregates still remain, the fruit of non-returning
（realizing the fruit of anāgāmin）
. Bhikkhus!
Needless to say seven years
, ... Bhikkhus!
Needless to say six years
, ... Bhikkhus!
Needless to say one year
, ... Bhikkhus!
Needless to say seven months
, ... Bhikkhus!
Needless to say one month
, ... Bhikkhus!
Needless to say half a month
, if anyone rightly cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness in this way for
seven days
, he may expect one of two kinds of fruit: the highest wisdom in this very life, or, if the five aggregates still remain, the fruit of non-returning.”

[The four fruits]Cultivating the four noble truths yields four fruits: the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arhatship. Of these, the fourth fruit, the arhat, is the highest. One who attains it is freed from birth and death and no longer receives a further existence.
As for the question whether
“within one day and night, even up to seven days and nights,

one can attain single-minded, unconfused recollection,” the answer is: single-minded, unconfused recollection is the state in which the myriad thoughts return to one, and the myriad thoughts returning to one is but the most elementary stage of practice. In terms of Chan, one must pass from the myriad thoughts returning to one, and from one returning to nothingness, to see one's nature and realize the mind,
then practice the nurturing of that attainment, until the delusions of views and thoughts are entirely cut off, and only then can one be free of birth and death and escape the cycle

. Therefore, some Chan practitioners have already brought the myriad thoughts to one, but are still far from seeing their nature and realizing the mind; once they hear of the excellence of the pure-land Dharma-gate and turn to Buddha-recitation, they can attain single-minded, unconfused recollection（single-minded, unconfused）
within one day and night, even up to seven days and nights

. Since ancient times there have been countless such instances; see in detail The Records of the Pure Land Sages and Worthies. And those Chan practitioners who have already seen their nature and realized the mind and turn to the pure-land Dharma-gate can attain single-minded, unconfused recollection within a single day; many of them later became great masters of the pure-land school, as is recorded in The Records of the Pure Land Sages and Worthies. For example, the Great Master Chewu, as the thirty-sixth patriarch of the Linji line, opened great lecture halls and led the assembly in Chan contemplation, encouraging later students with tireless zeal. For fourteen years without a break, his fame spread north and south, and the Chan style flourished greatly. But afterwards, whenever he recalled the Great Master Yongming（the sixth patriarch of the pure-land school）, himself a great master of the Chan line, who had nonetheless turned his heart to the pure land, reciting the Buddha's name a hundred thousand times a day, hoping to be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, he could not help reflecting: in this age of the Dharma's end, one should all the more follow Yongming's example. So he left the Chan monastery, devoted himself wholly to the pure land, taught countless beings, and thereby became the twelfth patriarch of the pure-land school.

As for those who study Buddhism but have not yet brought the myriad thoughts to one, the time will be longer; how long it takes precisely depends on each person's foundation and progress. Generally speaking, as long as the method is correct（for example, cultivating according to
Mindful Buddha-Recitation (Abridged Edition)

）, through diligent effort everyone can attain single-minded, unconfused recitation of the Buddha's name. This matter requires self-confidence（firm faith that one can attain single-minded, unconfused recollection）, perseverance, and fortitude. As for how self-confidence, perseverance, and fortitude can change one's destiny, Mr. Yu Jingyi has set us an excellent example; see in detail
The Record of Mr. Yu Jingyi Meeting the God of the Kitchen (Original Text and Colloquial Version)
（its annotations are in
The Annotated Record of Mr. Yu Jingyi Meeting the God of the Kitchen

Therefore, those who recite the Buddha's name must have true faith and sincere vows, and be diligent and unremitting. Though one labors diligently for a single life, it is but a moment; once one reaches the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, one's lifespan is immeasurable and one's bliss without end, and one attains Buddhahood and delivers sentient beings, fulfilling the great bodhi vow.

Here the World-honored One sets forth faith, vow, and practice with the utmost clarity: faith is believing and accepting this sutra (the dharma received and protected by all Buddhas); vow is resolving to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss; practice is cultivating as taught — keeping the mind fixed and unconfused. blocks.text: 5. Received and Protected by All Buddhas

inline.s: The previous chapter, “The Buddhas of the Ten Directions Praise,” and this chapter, “Received and Protected by All Buddhas,” together prove
that the Sutra of the Praise of the Pure Land Buddha-land, Received and Protected, is
(of course including also Amitābha Buddha)
praised by the Buddhas and
(of course including also Amitābha Buddha)

received and protected by the Buddhas. In other words, the Sutra of the Praise of the Pure Land Buddha-land, Received and Protected, is spoken by the golden mouth of our original teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha, and is the dharma praised and received-protected by Amitābha Buddha of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Therefore this sutra is the fundamental basis for the study and practice of the Pure Land school. Those who recite the Buddha’s name should practice as taught and be born in that Buddha-land.

Moreover, Sariputra, why is this sutra named “Praise of the Inconceivable Merits and Virtue of the Buddha-land, the Dharma Received and Protected by All Buddhas”? Sariputra, because in this sutra the merits and virtues of the inconceivable Buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life are proclaimed and praised, and the World-honored Buddhas of the ten directions, wishing by skillful means to bring benefit and bliss to all beings, each dwelling in his own land, display great miraculous transformations and speak words of truth, urging all beings to believe and accept this dharma. Therefore this sutra is named “Praise of the Inconceivable Merits and Virtue of the Buddha-land, the Dharma Received and Protected by All Buddhas.”

Then, Sariputra, for what reason is this sutra named “Praise of the Inconceivable Merits and Virtue of the Buddha-land, the Dharma Received and Protected by All Buddhas”? Sariputra, because in this sutra the merits and virtues of the inconceivable Buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life are proclaimed and praised, together with the World-honored Buddhas of the ten directions (of course also including Amitābha Buddha of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss), who, wishing by skillful means to bring benefit and bliss to all beings, each dwelling in his own land, display great miraculous transformations and speak sincerely and earnestly, urging all beings to believe and accept this dharma. Therefore this sutra is named “Praise of the Inconceivable Merits and Virtue of the Buddha-land, the Dharma Received and Protected by All Buddhas”.

Moreover, Sariputra, just as I now proclaim and praise, together with all the Buddhas, the inconceivable merits and virtues of the Buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, so the World-honored Buddhas of the ten directions also praise my inconceivable, boundless merits and virtues, all saying: Most rare and wonderful! Śākyamuni the Still, Sakya the Dharma-King, the Tathagata, the Worthy One, the Fully Enlightened One, Perfect in Wisdom and Conduct, the Well-Gone One, Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed Tamer, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha the World-honored One — that he should have been able, in this endurance world (Saha world), in the evil age of the five defilements, namely the defilement of the age, the defilement of beings, the defilement of afflictions, the defilement of views, the defilement of life, to attain anuttara-samyak-sambodhi therein, and for the sake of benefiting and bringing bliss to all beings through skillful means, to speak this dharma that is most difficult to believe in this world.

Śākyamuni the Dharma-King, the Tathagata, the Worthy One, the Fully Enlightened One, Perfect in Wisdom and Conduct, the Well-Gone One, Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed Tamer, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha the World-honored One — that he should have been able, in this Saha world, in the evil age of the five defilements (the defilement of the age, the defilement of beings, the defilement of afflictions, the defilement of views, the defilement of life), to attain anuttara-samyak-sambodhi therein, and for the sake of benefiting and bringing bliss to all beings through skillful means, to speak this dharma that is most difficult to believe in this world.

[Śākyamuni the Still]The two characters muni in Śākyamuni mean stillness. [Dharma-King]The Buddha is the lord of the Dharma-door, able to teach beings freely, and is therefore called Dharma-King. [Tamer]That is the Tamer of Men mentioned in the earlier notes. [The five defilements]First, the defilement of the age: the era encounters misfortune and disasters arise again and again; second, the defilement of afflictions: the minds of people are filled with greed, anger, and delusion; third, the defilement of beings (also called the defilement of beings): beings are of lowly capacity, with much suffering and little joy; fourth, the defilement of views: wrong views prevail and thought is in disorder; fifth, the defilement of life: beings receive retribution for evil karma, their bodies and minds are worn out, and their life-span is short. [The dharma most difficult to believe in the world]The Land of Ultimate Bliss is so supremely wondrous that one need only keep the mind fixed and unconfused to be reborn there by relying on the Buddha’s power and attain Buddhahood in a single lifetime. But how many people in the world truly believe and practice as taught? Therefore this is the dharma most difficult to believe in the world.

Therefore, Sariputra, know that I now, in this defiled endurance world, in the evil age of the five defilements, have attained anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, and for the sake of benefiting and bringing bliss to all beings through skillful means, have spoken this dharma that is most difficult to believe in this world — most rare, wonderful, and inconceivable.

Therefore, Sariputra, know that I now, in this defiled endurance world, the Saha world, in the evil age of the five defilements, have attained anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, and for the sake of benefiting and bringing bliss to all beings through skillful means, have spoken this dharma that is most difficult to believe in this world — most rare, wonderful, and inconceivable.

Moreover, Sariputra, in this defiled endurance world, in the evil age of the five defilements, if any good man or good woman of pure faith should hear this dharma, most difficult to believe in all the world, and can give rise to faith and understanding, receive it, uphold it, proclaim it, and practice as instructed — know that such a person is most rare, and has planted roots of goodness in the presence of countless Buddhas. At the end of life such a person will surely be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, enjoying the manifold merits and adornments of that pure Buddha-land and the joy of the Great Dharma; day and night, throughout the six periods, drawing near to and making offerings to the Buddha of Immeasurable Life; traveling through the ten directions and making offerings to all the Buddhas. In the presence of each Buddha, hearing the Dharma and receiving the prophecy, their stores of merit and wisdom will quickly be perfected, and they will quickly realize the unexcelled right and equal enlightenment.

Therefore, Sariputra, in this defiled endurance world, the Saha world, in the evil age of the five defilements, if any good man or good woman of pure faith should hear this Pure Land dharma, most difficult to believe in all the world, and can give rise to faith and understanding, receive it, uphold it, proclaim it, and practice as instructed — know that such a person is most rare, and has planted roots of goodness in the presence of countless Buddhas. At the end of life such a person will surely be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, enjoying the manifold merits and adornments of that pure Buddha-land and the joy of the Great Dharma; day and night, throughout the six periods, drawing near to and making offerings to the Buddha of Immeasurable Life; traveling through the ten directions and making offerings to all the Buddhas. In the presence of each Buddha, hearing the Dharma and receiving the prophecy, their stores of merit and wisdom will quickly be perfected, and they will quickly realize the unexcelled right and equal enlightenment.

[Receiving the prophecy]To receive from a Buddha the prediction that one will in the future certainly become a Buddha. [Merit and wisdom as provisions]The Buddha is complete in both merit and wisdom; therefore merit and wisdom are the provisions for attaining Buddhahood. [Provisions]Resources are the wealth, and provisions the food. Practicing the path is like a long journey: one must have the provisions of merit and wisdom in order to reach the destination. For those who recite the Buddha’s name and seek rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, it is necessary to have the three provisions of faith, vow, and practice.

At that time, when the Bhagavat had spoken this sutra, the Venerable Sariputra and the other great sravakas, together with the assemblies of bodhisattva mahasattvas, and immeasurable devas, humans, asuras, and others, all the great multitude, hearing what the Buddha had said, were filled with great joy, believed, accepted, and practiced it.
